caption:
Nvidia director Mark Stevens sold $946.6 million of Nvidia stock between August 31 and September 18, more than any other U.S. insider last quarter.
He sold at about $220 to $234 a share. Nvidia closed at $166.19 on November 12, the day Jensen Huang resigned.
No one has accused Stevens of wrongdoing, and his filings showed no prearranged trading plan.

Lucky timing or smart money?

paragraphs.text: Nvidia director Mark Stevens sold 4,236,740 shares of Nvidia stock for about $946.6 million between August 31 and September 18, 2026, according to SEC filings summarized by 24/7 Wall St. The sales were completed roughly seven to eleven weeks before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive on November 12, Moneywise reported on November 13.

According to Moneywise, the first round ran from August 31 to September 2 at prices between $220 and $226 a share and raised about $411 million. A second round on September 3 and 4, at $227 to $234 a share, brought in about $236 million. A final sale on September 18 at roughly $220 a share added about $300 million.

24/7 Wall St. reported that all of the sales went through a family trust and that the filings showed no prearranged Rule 10b5-1 trading plan, the kind of schedule executives often set up in advance so that later trades cannot be tied to inside knowledge. Moneywise noted that the absence of such a plan is not necessarily a red flag on its own, since insiders sell stock for many reasons, including raising cash.

A ranking published on October 7 found that no other U.S. insider sold as much stock in the third quarter. Arista Networks chief executive Jayshree Ullal was second with about $446.0 million, followed by CoreWeave chief executive Michael Intrator at about $347.2 million and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos at about $346.5 million, according to 24/7 Wall St.

Stevens also sold about $407 million of Nvidia stock in June, bringing his total since early summer to roughly $1.35 billion, the outlet reported. He still holds about 27.5 million shares. Huang made no open market sales over the summer.

Stevens is managing partner of S-Cubed Capital, a family office, and was a managing partner at Sequoia Capital from 1993 to 2011, according to Nvidia's board biography. He served as an Nvidia director from 1993 to 2006 and rejoined the board in 2008. He sits on the compensation committee and the nominating and corporate governance committee.

Huang stepped down after reports about his personal relationships, including an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese intelligence operative, Moneywise reported. The board named chief financial officer Colette Kress interim chief executive. Nvidia closed at $166.19 on November 12, about 30.5% below its record close of $239.24 on October 6, according to 24/7 Wall St., which said the stock fell 22.2% over ten trading days.

Josh Brown, chief executive of Ritholtz Wealth Management, warned on CNBC that a new leader could get the strategy wrong. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on November 17 with Kress as interim chief executive.

Nothing in the reporting suggests Stevens knew about the problems that later forced Huang out, and the first two rounds followed a strong second quarter report that lifted the stock. Still, a director selling close to a billion dollars without a preset plan, weeks before the company's worst leadership crisis, is the kind of timing shareholders notice. Measured against the November 12 close, the shares he sold were worth roughly a quarter less than the prices he received.
The November 17 earnings report is the first under Kress, and investors will watch whether new Form 4 filings show further sales by Stevens or other insiders.
